advantages.what: npm test asserts published perft through depth 3: start 8902, Kiwipete 97862, and position 3 at 2812, so pin, en-passant discovery, and promotion-capture regressions fail the suite that actually runs. X's suite stops at depth 2 (20/400 and 48/2039).
npm test enforces the depth-2 start-position budget: a 110 ms stall on the opening made TC-8 fail. The same class of stall left X's npm test green.
Invalid FENs are tested (null, no kings, bad rank width, bad fields) and must throw. X never passes an invalid FEN, so the parser contract is unguarded.
A non-string FEN throws TypeError 'Expected a FEN string', and two white kings throw 'Invalid FEN kings'. X raises an incidental trim TypeError and still returns moves for two kings.
X's non-string test fails a correct applyMove that string-coerces and then rejects, because it asserts Symbol.toPrimitive and toString are never called.
The README states that only an exact lowercase UCI string is accepted and that anything else throws IllegalMoveError. Y has no customer-facing note.
The README and the suite both cover a saved FEN: same moves, status, and result after another game, a rejected move, and a fresh process. Y behaves this way but does not document or test it.
X does not lock Y's exact invalid-FEN sentences, so parser wording can change. Y's TC-2 requires /Invalid FEN kings/, /Invalid FEN rank width/, and /Invalid FEN fields/.
X's spec states every stated requirement, including castling, en passant, promotion, and that npm test passes. Y's spec leaves S-33, S-34, S-35, and S-40 absent.

pairs.why: Y is the engine to keep because the suite npm test runs locks depth-3 move counts, the two-second budget, and invalid-FEN failures. X is the same correct rules engine, documents exact UCI and saved-FEN resume, tests that resume, and does not freeze parser sentences. Those missing guards are assertions plus a small validation change on an engine the audit already found correct through depth 4.
